Title: A single generic ‘Preserve Editorial Intent’ instruction caused consistent editorial drift and failed promotion
Description: Adding one generic section to the Narrative user prompt — “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” — produced reproducible regressions: company identity and audience scope were subordinated, orchestration became the central positioning, unsupported claims were introduced, and the candidate prompt was rejected and rolled back. The experiment shows that a seemingly small, generic constraint can materially harm downstream editorial fidelity in this pipeline.
Audience: Product managers, prompt engineers, editorial leads working with LLM-driven pipelines
Rationale: Why it matters: The team intended the rule to protect a brief’s top-level message, but the candidate prompt produced lower mean scores for both Narrative and Compose and failed hard gates (theme hierarchy and factual restraint). The decision recorded was explicit: “Do not promote,” and the baseline prompt was restored byte-for-byte. This is valuable for teams running prompt-change experiments because it demonstrates a concrete failure mode where a well-intentioned, general instruction produced measurable regressions. Gaps and uncertainty: the experiment used three runs per condition (not statistically large), no temperature/seed control was available, and the model alias may map to varying backends; those limits affect how broadly the result can be generalized.
Evidence:
Candidate prompt change: added a section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.”
Narrative mean scores: baseline 6.00/10, candidate 4.00/10. Compose mean scores: baseline 5.67/10, candidate 3.33/10.
Observed failures: candidate outputs “subordinated company identity and audience scope,” “made orchestration the central positioning,” and “introduced unsupported validation or audience framing.”
Decision: “Do not promote. Candidate was worse on mean score… failed the orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint gates… production prompt was restored.”
Rollback verification: production prompt SHA-256 restored exactly.
